newsitem.title: CANADA: Morrison seen mounting aggressive bid defense.
newsitem.headline: Morrison seen mounting aggressive bid defense.

text.p: Morrison Petroleums Ltd., the target of a C$652 million ($476 million) hostile takeover bid from Canadian 88 Energy Corp., is expected to mount an aggressive defense to the surprise offer.
Morrison Chairman Gordon Stollery brings to the fight a reputation for innovative financing since transforming his firm into an oil producer from a mining company in the late 1970s.

"He's got a lot of street smarts and he's going to fight this," said Peter Linder, analyst with brokerage CIBC Wood Gundy in Calgary. "I suggested to shareholders that there's a good possibility of another offer and that offer could also be some kind of reorganization...hold on to the stock."

Canadian 88, led by aggressive oilman Greg Noval, said on Monday it would offer C$10 ($7.30) cash, to a maximum of C$140 million ($102 million), or 1.5 Canadian 88 shares for each Morrison share. The deal was contingent on the voiding of a Morrison shareholder rights plan, just announced.
Morrison on Tuesday had yet to comment on the proposal and had not revealed its choice for financial adviser.

Analysts pegged Morrison's net asset value at below C$8 ($5.84) a share, the approximate market price late last year after the company reported disappointing results from its much-watched Racehorse Creek exploration gas well in the southwestern Alberta foothills.

Morrison and Canadian 88 are major players in gas exploration in the region, known for potentially rich reserves and expensive deep drilling. Canadian 88 stock has soared since the company announced a major discovery in the region last year.
How much more value Stollery might extract from Morrison was up for debate.

Ken Faircloth, analyst with Goepel Shields & Partners, projected a 12-month target price for Morrison of C$10 before the bid was announced. "To me, the C$10 number is a reasonable number. You might be able to get a little bit more but I don't think you can expect a lot more," Faircloth said.
After the bid was made public, market players suggested several rival bidders for Morrison might emerge.

Speculation also surfaced that Morrison, flush with cash after a series of asset sales and the creation of an income trust, could turn around and mount a bid for Canadian 88. But that strategy was derided on Tuesday.

Faircloth said that Morrison, with its recent history of disappointing stock returns, would have difficulty convincing Canadian 88 shareholders it could do a better job of managing high-flying Canadian 88's assets.

Market sources said Stollery, in an effort to boost the value of the company's various parts, may propose breaking the company into three, possibly creating an income fund for its Coleman, Alberta gas plant, a production royalty trust and an exploration company.
However, that would take time and Noval, whose brash style has generated controversy in Canada's oil patch, said on Monday he would walk away from the bid if it was not accepted.
Morrison was up C$0.05 to C$10 on the Toronto Stock Exchange on Tuesday, while Canadian 88 rose C$0.15 to C$6.60.
